events.text: A cloud has been lying on the ridge above the cave all morning, low and white and thick as new cotton. You have walked on water for a hundred and fifty years and have stopped noticing it. Now, at the edge of the ridge, your forehoof goes out over nothing, and the cloud dimples under it like a quilt, and holds.

choices.text: Step out onto it with all four hooves

effects.log: It holds. You stand on a cloud over the pines, and the cloud drifts, slowly, with you on it, out over the valley. Under you a woodcutter looks up at the sky for a long time and decides, wisely, to say nothing to his wife.

choices.text: Test it one hoof at a time, all day

effects.log: By dusk you know clouds: which ones are only fog, which ones would drop a sparrow, which ones would carry an army. The ones that carry you are the ones that would not feel an ant. Of course they are.

choices.text: Draw the hoof back. The ground has been kind to you

effects.log: You stay on the ridge for a season, on the grass you spent seven hundred years learning not to bend. Then one morning you step onto the cloud without thinking about it, the way you once stepped onto the river.

events.text: From the height of the clouds you can see every war at once. That is the trouble with it. A burning town in the east, a siege in the south, two sects fighting over a ford in the north, a famine column on a road in the west, and you, standing on a cloud, harming nothing, too far from all of them.

choices.text: Go down to the nearest, and do what a qilin can

effects.log: The nearest is the famine column. You walk ahead of it for a month, and the villages on the road open their granaries because a five-coloured beast is walking ahead of the hungry. It is one road of forty. (-6 health)

choices.text: Watch them all, and learn the shape of the age

effects.log: A whole season of watching. Wars are not separate things, you learn: the famine feeds the siege, the siege feeds the sect war, and the burning town was set alight by men from the famine column. Pull one thread and the others move.

choices.text: Look away. A qilin that sees everything can bear nothing

effects.log: You turn your back on the view and graze the dew off the top of the cloud, which tastes of nothing. It does not help. Some things, once seen from above, are seen for good.

events.text: A lark lands on the cloud beside you, very surprised to find it solid. It walks up and down, testing it, then looks at you with the expression of a bird who suspects this is your fault.

choices.text: Let it ride down with you to the meadow

effects.log: It rides the whole way down on the cloud, standing very straight, and gets off at the meadow without a word of thanks, which is how larks are. All summer it sings at a height no lark has ever sung at.

choices.text: Step off and leave it the cloud

effects.log: You step down onto the next cloud and leave the lark the whole of the first one. It sits in the middle of it like a magistrate and is carried away over the ridge, outraged and delighted.

events.text: High over the Nine-Step Palace, where no bird goes, you find them: hoofprints in the cloud, very old, very large, each one a small pool of light. Two sets, side by side, as if a beast carried something heavy and walked carefully. They go up, and up, and stop. The old qilin-horse went this way with the founder on its back, the night you were born.

choices.text: Put your hoof in one

effects.log: It fits. Long ago at the Morning-Heaven Stone it was far too big. Now it fits exactly, and you stand there with one hoof in the old print of the beast that bore you, if it did, and the cloud is warm.

choices.text: Follow them up to where they stop

effects.log: They stop at the edge of the blue. Nothing beyond, not a door, not a gate, only the place where a beast and a king stopped being something you could follow. You stand there until the cloud thins under you and you have to go down.

choices.text: Walk round them, so as not to spoil them

effects.log: You walk round them, the way you once walked round the ant road at the cave mouth. Somebody should keep them. The clouds will not, and you are the only other beast who knows they are here.

events.text: Word comes up the river the way word used to come in the oldest days: a messenger in a straw hat, asleep on their feet at the cave mouth. A king is dying downriver. Not a son of kings: a founder, who started with a borrowed horse and nine friends and ended with a kingdom. {npc} asks for nothing, the messenger says. Only that the beast of the cave come and look at {him} once, before the end.

choices.text: Go down the river to {him}

mem.note: came from the cave to my deathbed

effects.log: {npc} is lying in a plain room with the shutters open on the river. {He} looks at you a long time. "So it is true," {he} says. "The first one did not take the beast along. It left a foal."

choices.text: Send back word that a qilin comes for the birth of a sage, not for a king

effects.log: The messenger carries it back. A month later the messenger is at the cave mouth again, asleep standing up. "{npc} says {he} was born once too," comes the word, "and nobody came. {He} would like to make up for it." You go.

events.text: {npc} has had {his} bed carried to the window. Every evening {he} tells you a little more of the kingdom: the borrowed horse, the river crossing, the friends who are all dead now, the one battle {he} is ashamed of. Tonight {he} stops in the middle and says: "The first king rode the beast up from the stone and never came back. I want to go the same way. Will you carry me?"

choices.text: Say yes

effects.log: {npc} lets out a breath {he} has been holding for a year. "At the stone," {he} says. "Not here. I will not go up from a bed."

choices.text: Ask {him} why the founder never came back

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} coughs. "Because there was nothing up there worth coming back for," {he} says, "or because there was. I mean to find out which."

choices.text: Tell {him} you have carried souls across rivers, not kings into the sky

effects.log: "A king is a soul with a crown on," says {npc}. "Leave the crown here. My grandson wants it."

events.text: The night at the Morning-Heaven Stone. {npc} has been carried up from the river in a chair by four grandchildren who are trying not to cry, and set down on the flat stone before the cave, beside the old hoofprints. The rapids roar below. The temple bell above rings the hour. {He} puts {his} hand flat in one of the old prints, the way you put your hoof in it long ago, and says, "Well."

choices.text: Kneel, so {he} can climb onto your back

effects.log: {He} climbs on like a boy climbing onto a wall, and sits there, and does not say anything for a long while. The grandchildren stand very close together on the edge of the stone.

choices.text: Let the grandchildren say their goodbyes first, as long as they need

effects.log: It takes until the small hours. The youngest will not let go of {his} sleeve. {npc} tells the child the whole story of the borrowed horse, again, and at the end the child lets go.

events.text: {npc} is on your back on the Morning-Heaven Stone, and the sky above the cave is open the way it was the night you were born. You could go up. You can feel the way: the cloud waiting over the rapids, the old prints of light in the sky, the place where the blue begins. If you go, you will not come back either. Nobody does. {npc} leans forward and says, very quietly, "Only if you want to."

choices.text: Carry {him} up as far as the clouds, and bring {him} down again to die among {his} own

mem.note: rode the beast to the edge of heaven and came home

effects.npcPass: old age, on the Morning-Heaven Stone
effects.log: You climb the night until the river is a thread and the kingdom is a smudge of lamps, and you let {him} look at all of it. Then you bring {him} down. {He} dies at dawn on the stone with {his} grandchildren round {him}, laughing at something. In the morning there is a new set of hoofprints in the rock beside the old ones.

choices.text: Tell {him} you cannot. You have sages still to see home

effects.npcPass: old age, on the Morning-Heaven Stone
effects.log: {npc} nods as if {he} expected it. "Then carry me to the edge of the stone," {he} says, "so I can see the rapids." You do. {He} dies looking at the water, and that is the way {he} goes up, in the end.

choices.text: Go up from the stone, and do not come back

effects.log: You go up from the stone with the king on your back, and the cloud takes you, and the stone keeps your hoofprints beside the old ones. A thousand years later a poet climbs the pavilion above the rapids on a night with a sliver of moon and writes that the qilin-horse went and did not return. Two sets of prints, now. Nobody can tell which is older.

events.text: The kingdom the founder left has a new custom. On the night the old king died, every year, the grandchildren's grandchildren climb to the Morning-Heaven Stone with lamps, and put their hands in the hoofprints, and tell the story of the borrowed horse to whichever child is youngest. Then they look up the cliff at the cave mouth, in case.

choices.text: Stand in the cave mouth where the lamps can reach you, once

effects.log: The youngest child sees you first and does not shout. The others turn, and the lamps come up, and for a moment a whole family is looking at you in silence, the way the founder looked at you, as if checking a story against the world. Then the child waves.

choices.text: Stay in the dark and let them tell it

effects.log: The story has grown in the telling. Now the founder rode a qilin up to heaven and came back with the dawn, which is almost exactly true, and much better told than you could tell it.

events.text: A poet on the pavilion above the rapids, in a cold autumn with the city half empty after a war. The moon is a sliver. The poet is writing, and says the lines aloud as they come, to nobody: the qilin-horse went and did not return; where does the heavenly grandson wander? You are standing on the water below, in the dark.

choices.text: Stay where you are, and let the poem be true

effects.log: The poem goes into the books. For centuries scholars quote it whenever a good thing is gone. You are not gone. But the poem is about absence, and absence is real, and you would not take it away from them.

choices.text: Let the moonlight find you, for one breath, on the water

effects.log: The poet sees five colours on the dark water below the pavilion and stops in the middle of a line. When the moon comes out again there is nothing on the river. The poet finishes the line exactly as planned, and adds a note in the margin that nobody can read afterwards.

events.text: Something in your throat that was not there before: a weight, smooth and cool, like a river stone you swallowed in your sleep. It does not hurt. It is waiting. And somewhere to the south, in a village by a slow river, a woman who has climbed a hill to pray for a child has just come down it again, and you know, the way you knew each of the five, that the last sage is coming. The one without a colour.

choices.text: Go south at once, and wait by the river

effects.log: You find the village by the smell of the river and the sound of a loom. The house is the poorest on the lane. You lie down in the reeds across the water and wait, and the weight in your throat grows heavier and cooler.

choices.text: Ask yourself what a sage with no colour is for

effects.log: Blue taught, red healed, yellow waited, white mourned, black judged. You go through them all on the cloud, and come to the end of the colours, and understand: this one will gather them. A king without a throne. You go south.

events.text: The woman's time has come, at dusk, in the poorest house on the lane. You stand at the gate. The weight in your throat rises, and you open your mouth, and it comes out: a tablet of jade the length of a hand, green as river water, and on it, in characters nobody carved, a child of the essence of water, who will carry on a failing age as a king without a throne.

choices.text: Lay it on the threshold, where the midwife will find it

effects.log: The midwife finds it and drops the water bucket. The woman inside asks what is wrong, and the midwife reads it aloud to her in a shaking voice, and the woman, between pains, starts to laugh.

choices.text: Hold it in your mouth until the child cries

effects.log: The jade is cold and heavy and tastes of the river. The child cries at midnight. You set the tablet down on the step, and your throat aches for a year. (-5 health)

choices.text: Swallow it back. Nobody should be told who they will be

ok.log: You swallow it. It will not stay down. In the morning it is on the step anyway, and you understand that the book was never yours to keep, only to carry.

fail.log: You try. The jade sticks halfway and you cough it onto the step in front of the midwife, which is not how the omen was meant to go. (-8 health)

events.text: The mother has the child in her arms and the jade book in her lap. She has no ribbon in five colours. She has a length of plain undyed silk from the loom, the first thing she ever wove, and she comes out to the gate on the first morning and ties it round your horn, as the old women say you must. You stay two nights.

choices.text: Lower your head for the ribbon

mem.note: stood at the gate when I was born

effects.log: Plain silk on a horn that has worn five colours. It is the lightest ribbon you have ever carried and the heaviest. On the second night you hear {npc} cry in the house, and the mother sing, and the river answer, and you leave before dawn.

choices.text: Lie at the gate both nights, so the whole lane can see you

mem.note: stood at my gate where the whole lane saw

effects.log: The whole lane comes to look, and then the whole village, and then a magistrate who writes it down. {npc} grows up with every door in the village open, because everyone was there the night the beast lay at the gate.

events.text: {npc} is grown, and teaching. Not in a palace. Under a ginkgo at the edge of a market town, to anyone who sits down: farmers' children, a retired soldier, two runaway disciples of a sword sect, a magistrate's clerk on {his} day off. They say there are three thousand of them now. {npc} keeps the jade book in a plain box and never opens it. "I know what it says," {he} tells the students. "It does not say how."

choices.text: Lie in the shade at the back of the class, unseen, for a season

effects.log: You listen to {npc} teach. It is not about the five colours. It is about how to be a person when the age is bad. Half of it is things you learned by not doing them. You find yourself nodding, which is hard to do invisibly.

choices.text: Let {him} see you, once, at the back of the class

mem.note: saw the beast of the jade book at the back of my class

effects.log: {npc} sees you over the heads of three thousand students and stops in the middle of a sentence. Then {he} finishes it. Afterwards {he} says nothing to anyone, but the next lesson is about gratitude, and it is the best {he} ever gives.

choices.text: Stand guard over the town when the sword sects come to recruit

effects.log: The recruiters come at harvest. You stand in the road. They go round you, and the students do not follow them. {npc} never learns why that year's recruiters left empty-handed. (-6 health)

events.text: {npc} is old, and the students have copied the jade book a thousand times, and every copy is only words. "They read it and they hear nothing," {he} tells you at night under the ginkgo, the only one who ever speaks to you as if you were a neighbour. "The first one rang. You could hear it. If a voice were in it, every child who opened it would hear what I heard." {He} does not ask. {He} would never ask.

choices.text: Keep your voice, and teach the students yourself, once

effects.log: One lesson under the ginkgo, in the bell voice, to three thousand students who will tell it for the rest of their lives. It is not the book. It is enough. {npc} sits at the back and listens like a child.

choices.text: Tell {him} the book was never meant to ring. People are

effects.log: {npc} is quiet a long time. Then {he} laughs, softly, so as not to wake the students sleeping in the hall. "That is the first thing anyone has taught me in forty years," {he} says. {He} writes it on the inside of the box lid.

choices.text: Give your voice to the book

effects.log: You open your mouth over the plain box, and what comes out is not jade this time. It is the bell. It goes into the book and stays there. You are the words now. For two thousand years, every schoolchild who opens that book on the first morning hears, very faintly, a temple bell at dawn, and sits up straighter, and does not know why.

events.text: The black ribbon. You heralded this one at a stranger gate than any of the others: a prison, where a woman taken for her husband's debts gave birth on the straw, and the guards stood in the corridor not knowing where to look. The child grows up in the prison until the age of six, and learns the sound of every door in it, and every kind of crying.

choices.text: Stand outside the bars every night of those six years

effects.log: Six winters outside a prison wall. The guards get used to the shape in the rain and leave the window shutter open for it. The child talks to you through the bars and you listen. (-5 health)

choices.text: Speak to the warden, once, in the bell voice

ok.log: The warden listens with his hat in his hands. The mother is released within the month. The child walks out of the prison gate at five, looking back, as if leaving home.

fail.log: The warden listens, and is moved, and has no power at all. He brings the mother a blanket. It is something. The child stays until six.

events.text: {npc}, the child of the black ribbon, is a magistrate now, the youngest in the province, and the first act of {his} first morning is to walk into the interrogation room, look at the cudgels, the leg-screws and the rack, and have them carried out into the yard and burned. The clerks say it cannot be done. Confessions come from the room.

choices.text: Stand in the yard by the fire, where the clerks can see you

effects.log: The clerks see a beast of five colours standing by the fire of burning cudgels, and stop arguing. Within a year the province has fewer confessions and fewer wrong ones, and the clerks have learned to ask questions, slowly, which is harder.

choices.text: Walk beside {him} that night, unseen, all the way home

effects.log: {npc} walks home alone after dark through the market. You walk behind {him}. Three men are waiting in an alley with a sack. They see what is behind {him}, and do not come out.

events.text: A noble whose steward was hanged on {npc}'s verdict has hired killers. You know because you can hear them: three of them, on the roof of the court at night, very quiet, waiting for the magistrate to work late, which {npc} always does. You cannot fight. You have never fought.

choices.text: Stand under the eaves in plain sight and look up at them

ok.log: Three killers on a roof look down and see a five-coloured beast looking up at them, very calmly, as if it had all night. They have all night too. By dawn they have decided, one by one, that they do not.

fail.log: One of them throws a knife at you to see if you are real. You are. You do not move. The knife in your flank decides them better than your eyes did: they go, leaving a beast bleeding quietly under the eaves. (-12 health)

choices.text: Go in and lie down across the magistrate's door

effects.log: They come down at the second watch and find the door blocked by something they cannot step over and cannot move. One of them tries a blade on it. You bear it. They leave before the bell, and {npc} comes out in the morning to find blood on the step and nobody hurt but you. (-10 health)

choices.text: Knock them off the roof (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One step onto the tiles and the roof is clear. The third one does not get up from the yard. {npc} is safe. In the still water of the court's well, next morning, the tip of your horn looks paler than it did. (Bent +10)

events.text: They have caught one of the noble's killers, and {npc} has the name of the noble already, and no proof. The clerks have brought one cudgel back from somewhere. Just one. Just for this. {npc} is standing in the interrogation room looking at it, and has been for an hour.

choices.text: Speak to {him} through the window in the bell voice

ok.log: One sentence. {npc} puts the cudgel down, and goes and gets the killer a bowl of soup, and sits with them until morning. By dawn the killer has told {him} everything, for the soup and the sitting. The black ribbon holds.

fail.log: {npc} hears you and does not turn round. In the end {he} does not use the cudgel. {He} breaks it over {his} knee instead, and gets nothing out of the killer, and the noble goes free. The black ribbon holds, but only just.

choices.text: Stand in the doorway, so {he} has to look at you first

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. Then {he} laughs, a short unhappy laugh, and hands the cudgel to the clerk. "Burn it with the others," {he} says. The ribbon on your horn, which had begun to fray, lies flat again.

choices.text: Do nothing. It has to be {his} choice

ok.log: You wait outside in the rain. After a long time the door opens, and {npc} throws the cudgel out into the yard, into the mud. You were right not to. You were lucky to be right.

fail.log: You wait outside in the rain, and the sounds begin. By morning {npc} has the proof, and has become what {he} burned. The black ribbon tears on your horn before {he} comes out of the room.

events.text: {npc} is dying in a courtroom. Not {his} own: the provincial high court, where {he} has come, old, to argue one last case for a woman taken for a husband's debts, and has sat down in the middle of the speech, and not got up. They have laid {him} on the clerks' bench. The judges have not left. Nobody has told them to.

choices.text: Walk into the court

effects.log: Every head turns. You walk down the middle of the court, past the judges, past the woman in chains, to the clerks' bench. {npc} sees you and smiles like a child at a prison window. (The Last Appearance: be at the deathbed, and the black comes home.)

choices.text: Wait outside the window, as you did when {he} was small

effects.log: You stand in the rain outside the high court's window. {npc} turns {his} head toward it, as if {he} could hear the bars that are not there. (The Last Appearance: be at the deathbed, and the black comes home.)

events.text: In the still water below the rapids, for the first time in all your centuries, there is no grey on you. Blue, red, yellow, white, black, and the belly yellow. Five sages, from birth to death, every one of them. The coat is complete. It is the strangest thing to look at, and it is you.

choices.text: Stand and look until the light goes

effects.log: You stand there until dusk takes the colours one by one, black last. You remember each of them by name: the child who read before walking, the one who sat with the dying, the heir who waited, the shaman among the cairns, the judge at the prison window.

choices.text: Go and stand where each of them is buried, one by one

effects.log: Five graves, five provinces, a year. At each one you lower your head until the colour of them touches the grass. Nobody sees you do it. It is the only ceremony you have ever held. (-6 health)

events.text: Something has changed in the forest. You noticed it at the stream this morning: a wolf drinking, and a roe deer drinking beside it, and neither of them looking up. Then a fox and a hen, on the same path. Then a hawk on a branch over a nest of finches, asleep. The old book said: with the qilin kept, the beasts do not bolt. You did not know it meant this.

choices.text: Walk through the forest slowly, so it spreads

effects.log: It spreads behind you like a smell of rain. For three valleys the animals drink together, and a hunter who comes up the ridge that autumn sits down on a stump and cannot think why he brought the bow.

choices.text: Worry about the wolf, which has to eat

effects.log: The wolf eats, in the end. Not that morning, and not at the stream. It is not peace you have brought; it is a pause. But a pause at a stream is where a great many things begin.

events.text: A lord's hunt in the hills, with forty dogs. The dogs come over the ridge in full cry, see you in the clearing, five colours, no grey, and stop. All forty of them. Then, one by one, they lie down in the grass with their chins on their paws, and the huntsmen behind them pull up their horses and do not know what to do.

choices.text: Walk away through the dogs, very slowly

effects.log: You walk out of the clearing between forty lying dogs, and not one lifts its head. The lord, on his horse, takes off his hat. He goes home and never hunts in those hills again, and nobody asks him why, because they all saw it.

choices.text: Lie down among them

effects.log: You lie down in the grass among the dogs. The huntsmen get off their horses, after a while, and sit down too. By noon the whole hunt is having its lunch in a clearing with a beast of five colours, and the lord is telling a story about his grandmother.

events.text: Word from the Four Spirits, and it comes the way such word comes to a qilin: one morning every beast on the mountain is lying down facing the same way, south and up. The deer. The boar. A tiger, two ridges over, very embarrassed about it. The furred beasts were kept from bolting by you. Now something is keeping you. Come and be read.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Go at once

effects.log: You step up onto the cloud. Behind you, for the first time in a century, the beasts of the mountain get up and scatter, as beasts should. The tiger is the first to go, and does not look back.

choices.text: Go round every sage's grave first

effects.log: Whatever they ask you up there, you mean to have stood at each grave first. It takes a season. The beasts wait the whole season facing south, which is very patient of them.

choices.text: Ask why a beast that never fought should be read at all

effects.log: Nobody answers. The beasts go on facing south. After a month you understand that the question is the reason, and go.

events.text: At the top of the light there is a door made of weather: two pillars of white cloud and a lintel of mist, and beyond it a blue too deep to have a name. Nobody is there. Nobody asks you in. You stand on the threshold, and then, because standing is what you are good at, you go on standing.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Wait to be asked in

effects.log: You wait. Years. Behind you, on the cloud, your hoofprints fill with light, one by one, the way the old ones over the cave did. A long time later something else comes up the light to the door, a bird of five colours perhaps, and finds them, and wonders who stood here so long.

choices.text: Walk to the edge of nothing beyond the door, and look down at every land at once

effects.log: From the edge you can see all of it: every war, every sage's grave, every meadow you ever crossed. You stand there thinking until you forget you are waiting. When you turn round, the door is open.

events.text: It takes a tortoise eleven years to climb into the sky, and this one did it a very long time ago and has never gone down: a black tortoise as big as a threshing floor, a black serpent coiled round its shell, a long writing brush under the serpent's coils. "The qilin," says the tortoise. "Has never once been late," says the serpent. "Or early," they finish together. "Bring your ribbons. We already know them."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Bow to the Tortoise

effects.log: You bow so low your horn touches the cloud. The serpent says it has never seen a beast bow without bending anything before. The tortoise says it has, once, and they argue about it until evening.

choices.text: Ask who will ask the questions, since that seat is yours

effects.log: "We will," says the tortoise. "Badly," says the serpent. "Nobody has ever asked the qilin anything," they finish. "We have been practising." The serpent's laugh is a dry sound like ice cracking on a river.

choices.text: Tell them every ribbon by name before they can read it

effects.log: You name them all, the home ones and the torn and the faded, every one. The tortoise checks them against the shell and finds you have not missed one. The serpent finds you have been kinder to yourself than the shell is about one. It does not say which.

events.text: The Court of the Four Spirits sits on the same cloud terrace among the stars where the four directions hold their council, on the nights the directions are not sitting. At the edges a blue storm and a white frost lean in to watch: the guardians of the east and the west, who are not spirits and know it. In the centre a coil of gold cloud lies with its eyes shut: the Yellow Dragon, which listens with the patience of farmland. Two seats are empty. One is the seat of the one who comes, and nobody is coming tonight. The other is the seat of the one who asks. It is yours, and you are standing in front of it to be read.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Stand still in the middle of the terrace

effects.log: You stand. The cloud does not bend. The Yellow Dragon does not open its eyes, but its breathing changes, slowly, like wind over barley that has noticed something.

choices.text: Walk once round the empty seats, slowly

effects.log: Round the seat of the one who asks, and the seat of the one who comes. Without anybody telling you, you know that the first is yours and the second is a bird's, and that it is often empty, because worthy reigns are rare.

choices.text: Speak, and find out what your voice sounds like up here

effects.log: Not the bell. The bell is for humans. Up here your voice comes out like rain on a thatched roof, and the serpent stops talking in the middle of a word to listen to it.

events.text: The tortoise asks the first question, slowly, and the serpent asks it again, faster, because the tortoise asked it wrong: "How many did you harm?" The serpent unrolls the inside of the shell. The count is there. It has always been there. Every blade, every beetle, every stampede, every wound, kept by somebody who was not you.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Say the number before they read it

effects.log: You say it. The tortoise reads it. They are the same. The serpent looks almost disappointed. "The ones who know their own count," says the tortoise, "are rarer than the ones with none."

choices.text: Ask them to read every one aloud

effects.log: It takes a month. Every one of them, read aloud on a terrace among the stars: every blade and every beetle, all of it. You do not look away once. The Yellow Dragon, which was asleep, says, "Good," without opening its eyes. (-5 health)

events.text: The tortoise asks the first question, slowly, and the serpent asks it again, faster: "How many did you harm?" The serpent unrolls the inside of the shell, and keeps unrolling it, looking for the place, and comes to the end, and looks at the tortoise, and the tortoise looks at you. The page is empty. Not one blade.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: Nobody says anything for a long time. Then the serpent laughs, the ice-cracking laugh, and the tortoise does not tell it to stop. The blue storm at the edge of the terrace, very quietly, rains.

choices.text: Say that the vow cost other people, even so

effects.log: "The village you could not defend," you say. "The city you would not strike for." The Yellow Dragon opens one eye. "Yes," it says. "That is the true count. Keep it." It shuts the eye again, and the terrace is very warm.

events.text: The second question is about the ribbons that are not home. The tortoise lays them out on the cloud the way the shell remembers them: the torn ones, where a sage you heralded took up the sword "for peace", and the faded ones, where a sage died and you were not there. They are very small, laid out like that. They do not feel small.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Tell the court each sage's name, and what became of them

effects.log: You tell them. Some of it is shameful and some of it is only sad. The serpent writes the shameful parts in red and the sad parts in black, and asks you twice which was which.

choices.text: Ask whether a torn ribbon is the qilin's fault or the sage's

effects.log: "Both," says the tortoise. "Neither," says the serpent. "It is the age's," they finish, and then argue about it for a week, and you are not sure they have ever agreed about anything faster.

choices.text: Ask to go back down and herald another of each colour

effects.log: "You may," says the tortoise. "The court will wait," says the serpent. The Yellow Dragon breathes out, long, which you have learned means yes, and also means it is pleased you asked.

events.text: The Yellow Dragon opens its eyes, both of them, which nobody on the terrace has seen it do in a century, and asks the only question it will ask: "A dragon brings rain. A phoenix comes to a worthy reign. The Tortoise keeps the record. You never fought anything. Why should a beast that never fought sit among us?"
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: "I do not know that it should"

effects.log: The Yellow Dragon looks at you a long time. "Good," it says at last. "The ones who know already are the ones we have to replace." It shuts its eyes. The terrace lets out its breath.

choices.text: "Because someone at this table should be the one who did not"

effects.log: "That is an answer," says the Yellow Dragon. "Not the answer." But it does not shut its eyes for the rest of the night, and in the morning there is barley growing at the edge of the terrace where there was only cloud.

choices.text: Lower your head, so it can see the tip of your horn

effects.log: It looks at the tip of your horn, where the flesh is, soft as a foal's mouth after all these centuries. It looks for a long time. Then it says, very quietly, to the whole terrace: "There. That is why."

events.text: From the east edge of the terrace the blue storm leans in, and it is the Azure Dragon, whose valley you once lived in, and it speaks for you without being asked, which guardians are not supposed to do at the Spirits' court. "In my valley," it says, "there were no wars for as long as the qilin lay on my ridge. I took the credit. It was the qilin's."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Bow to the storm

effects.log: You bow to the east. The storm rumbles, embarrassed, and rains a little on the Yellow Dragon by accident. The Yellow Dragon does not mind. The tortoise writes it all down, including the rain.

choices.text: Tell the court the valley's peace was the dragon's too

effects.log: "Both," you say. The storm goes quiet. The serpent says it has never seen two beasts try to give each other the credit before, and that it is very bad for the record, and writes both names on the same line.

events.text: Nobody speaks for you. The blue storm at the east edge is only weather tonight, and the white frost at the west edge is only cold. The serpent looks at the tortoise. "Usually," it says, "someone speaks." "Usually," says the tortoise, "someone has fought beside them."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Speak for yourself, in the voice like rain

effects.log: You speak. Not of yourself: of the sages, one by one, and of the meadows. It sounds, the serpent says afterwards, exactly like rain on a thatched roof, which is to say that nobody remembers the words and everybody slept better.

choices.text: Let the silence speak

effects.log: You stand in it. The silence goes on until it stops being a silence and becomes something else, like snow becoming a field. At the end the Yellow Dragon says "Yes," to nobody in particular, and the tortoise writes it down.

events.text: A witness is called: {npc}, a human of the upper heavens in robes of white cloud, who bows to you as if you had met, because you have. "In my first life," {npc} tells the court, "I was born in a poor house, and my mother tied a blue ribbon to the horn of a beast at the gate. I was the first. I want the court to know that it came back to my deathbed a lifetime later, and I knew it at once."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Let {him} tell it all

mem.note: bore witness for the Qilin before the Four Spirits

effects.log: {npc} tells it: the gate, the two nights, the village school that threw {him} out, the three thousand students, and the beast at the end, waiting for {him} to untie the ribbon with old fingers. The tortoise writes it in the serpent's hand, which is the better hand.

choices.text: Ask {him} whether {he} ever wished you had stayed

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it in front of the Four Spirits. "Every year," {he} says. "That is how I knew you were right to go." The Yellow Dragon opens both eyes for this, and keeps them open.

events.text: You take your seat on the terrace: the seat of the one who asks. The Tortoise, which records. The Yellow Dragon, which listens. Your own seat. And the seat of the one who comes, empty, waiting for a worthy reign. The tortoise dips its brush and says, "Then ask." "Anything," says the serpent. "We have not been asked anything in a very long time."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: "How many did you harm?"

effects.log: The tortoise and the serpent look at each other, and then, for the first time in their record, at their own shell. It takes them a century to answer. They answer honestly, and the Yellow Dragon says "Good," and it is the court's first hearing with you in it.

choices.text: "Where is the bird who should sit there?"

effects.log: "Below," says the Yellow Dragon, "waiting for a reign that deserves it." "It may be a long wait," says the tortoise. "It is always a long wait," says the serpent. You find you do not mind waiting. You were made for it.

choices.text: Ask nothing yet. Listen for a century first

effects.log: You sit, and listen, and do not ask. At the end of the century the Yellow Dragon, without opening its eyes, says that it has never sat beside anyone who listened as well as it does, and that it does not entirely like it.

events.text: A phoenix comes up the column of light to be read: five colours of feathers, a tail as long as a river, the measured dance of the courtyards still in its step. It lands on the terrace and stands waiting, the way you once stood. The seat of the one who comes. The asking is yours. You walk round it slowly, three times, and the cloud does not bend under you.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: "Every reign you came for. Which of them did not deserve you?"

effects.log: The bird answers. Some of it is honest and some of it is hope. You listen with your head low. "Knowing is the half of it," you tell it, and the tortoise writes the answer down for a long time, or for no time at all.

choices.text: "And the ones you missed?"

effects.log: At the edge of the terrace, thin as steam, the worthy who died without seeing it. The bird looks at them a long time. "A phoenix cannot be everywhere," it says. "No," you say. "Nor can a qilin. That is why there are four of us."

choices.text: Say nothing, and walk the circle with it instead

effects.log: It matches your steps without being asked, the measured dance against the walk that bends nothing. At the third turn you laugh, which you have not done in this court before. The serpent says it sounds like spring water. The Yellow Dragon opens one eye.

events.text: The Yellow Dragon comes to you alone at the edge of the terrace one evening, after long sittings, and lies down beside you on the cloud the way a field lies beside a road. "You could stay," it says. "In this seat, for good. Whenever an age is at peace, the beasts of the world would not run from the humans in it. Or you could go on. There is a further shape for a qilin. Very few have taken it. I do not know what it costs."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Go on toward the further shape

effects.log: "Then go," says the Yellow Dragon, "and come back and tell me." It shuts its eyes, and you understand that it will be awake the whole time you are gone.

choices.text: Ask for another century to decide

effects.log: "A century is short," says the tortoise. "For a deer it is long," says the serpent. The Yellow Dragon says nothing, and lies beside you, and the century begins.

choices.text: Stay, and take the seat for good

effects.log: You stay. The terrace takes your weight the way a meadow takes a hoof, and does not bend. From now on, whenever an age under heaven is at peace, a deer drinks beside a hunter at a stream, and neither looks up, and neither knows why it is not afraid.

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court has come to audit the Four Spirits, as it audits the four guardians: every coming, every reign, every land, every century accounted for. It has a retinue of clerks and a ledger bound in yellow silk. The Tortoise produces its shell. The Yellow Dragon produces a rain, a small one, over the envoy, as a courtesy. The envoy wipes its face and turns to you: "And the qilin? What has the qilin to show?"

choices.text: Produce a single blade of grass, unbent

effects.log: You lay it on the open ledger: one green blade from the meadow below the cave, standing straight on the page. The clerks stop writing. The tortoise writes, in its neatest characters: Grass, one blade. Unbent. Received. Somewhere below the shell, the serpent is laughing like ice on a river.

choices.text: Produce nothing. A qilin leaves no mark

effects.log: You stand there with nothing. The envoy waits. The clerks wait. After a long time the envoy writes Nothing in the ledger, and then looks at the word, and then, very carefully, underlines it twice. Every audit after this one, you decide, you will produce nothing at all.

choices.text: Take the envoy down to walk across a meadow behind you

effects.log: You walk the envoy across the meadow below the cave at dawn. Behind you the dew is gone from the grass, and the grass is standing. Behind the envoy it is flat. The envoy looks back at the two trails for a long time and stops writing.

events.text: The audit goes on for a decade and comes at last to the faded ribbons and the torn ones, and to the times you did not go: the villages you could not defend because a qilin does not fight, the city you would not strike for. The clerks have a separate ledger for these, bound in white hemp, and they handle it as if it were cold.

choices.text: Answer for every line in the white ledger

effects.log: You answer for each one. Some of them you would do again and say so. The envoy writes your answers in its own hand, not a clerk's, and at the end closes the white ledger gently, like a door on a sickroom.

choices.text: Ask the envoy what it would have done

effects.log: The envoy opens its mouth and shuts it. It has never been asked. It takes a week to answer, and the answer is long, and honest, and the tortoise writes it in the margin of your page, where it stays.

events.text: The audit is concluded. The envoy is packing its ledgers, and it shows you, before it closes the yellow book, the last line it wrote on your page: Harmed little. Waited much. Came when it was safe for others, not for itself. Received.

choices.text: Ask who audits the Jade court

effects.log: The envoy goes very still. The clerks stop packing. The Tortoise, to everyone's surprise, laughs out loud with both heads. The envoy leaves an hour early.

choices.text: Thank the envoy, and mean it

effects.log: Nobody has thanked an envoy of the Jade court in all the ages. It does not know what to do with its hands. It bows, badly, and goes, and the next audit is the gentlest the Spirits have ever had.

events.text: A hard age, and a lord in the west who rules by the sword has called a great hunt to show the provinces he can. Beaters by the thousand, dogs, nets on every ridge. You have been seen, in this age, which you should not have been, and the omen-readers in the towns say a beast of five colours seen now means a death.

choices.text: Go up onto the clouds until the hunt is over

effects.log: You go up. The hunt beats every valley for a month and finds deer and boar and a very old bear, and goes home, and the lord tells the provinces it found nothing worth taking. You come down when the dogs are gone.

choices.text: Stay on the ridge. The villages below need to see a beast that is not afraid

effects.log: You stay on the ridge in plain sight. The villages see you. So do the beaters. By the third day the whole hunt is turning toward your ridge, slowly, like a net being drawn in.

choices.text: Walk down among the beaters and speak to them in the bell voice

ok.log: A hundred beaters stop with their sticks raised. You talk to them for an evening. In the morning half of them have gone home to their fields, and the hunt is very much smaller than the lord would like.

fail.log: They listen, and they are poor men paid by the day, and the lord's steward is standing behind them with the pay chest. They raise the sticks again. You leave. They follow.

events.text: The net comes down in a ravine at dusk, silk cord as thick as a thumb, and a snare in the stream bed takes your foreleg and does what snares do. You are on the ground. The beaters stand round you in a ring with their sticks, and none of them knows what you are. One says a deer. One says a horse with a sickness. One says leave it.

choices.text: Lie still and let them take you

effects.log: They tie your legs and lift you into a cart. Nobody strikes you; they are too afraid, and too puzzled. The cart goes west, toward the lord's courtyard, with a ribbon on your horn swinging at every rut. (-15 health)

choices.text: Stand up on three legs and walk out through them

ok.log: You stand. They step back, every one of them, the way people step back from a thing they do not understand. You walk out of the ring on three legs and up onto the cloud, and nobody follows. (-12 health)

fail.log: You stand, and the leg gives, and you go down again, and this time they have the ropes on you before you can get up. The cart comes. (-18 health)

choices.text: Kick free of the snare (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One kick. The snare's stake comes out of the stream bed and takes the beater holding it across the face. He goes down bleeding. You are gone. In the still water of the next stream, the tip of your horn looks paler. (Bent +3; -8 health)

events.text: The lord's courtyard, in autumn. You lie in the cart with your foreleg bound in rope. The lord walks round you twice and does not know what you are. Nor do his scholars, nor his hunters, nor his omen-readers. One says it is a bad sign and should be killed. One says it is a good sign and should be caged. The lord says he will decide after dinner.

choices.text: Look at each of them, one by one, and wait

effects.log: You look at each of them. The scholar who said kill it cannot hold your eyes and goes to the back of the crowd. It is not much. It is what a beast in a cart can do.

choices.text: Speak to the lord in the bell voice

ok.log: One sentence. The lord goes white, and then red, and then orders the ropes cut and the cart taken back to the hills, and stops the hunt, and is quiet at dinner. For a year the west is a little gentler, and nobody can say why.

fail.log: The lord laughs, delighted. A beast that talks is better than a beast that does not. He orders a stronger cage.

events.text: An old sage pushes through the crowd in the courtyard: {npc}, very old now, whose birth you heralded at a gate with a ribbon. {He} sees the ribbon on your horn. {He} knows it at once. {He} lifts {his} sleeve to {his} face and weeps into it until the sleeve is wet through, and says, to nobody: "For whom have you come? For whom? My way is at an end."

choices.text: Lift your head, so {he} can see you are not finished

effects.log: You lift your head and look at {npc}. {He} stops weeping. {He} turns to the lord and, in a voice nobody in the west knew {he} had, names you, and tells the lord what it means that you were taken in that hunt. By morning the ropes are cut. {He} walks beside the cart all the way to the hills.

choices.text: Ask {him}, in the bell voice, to finish the book

effects.log: "Not at an end," you say. "Finish it." {npc} stares at you, and then laughs through the tears, and goes home and writes for ten more years. The lord, unnerved by a weeping sage and a talking beast, lets the cart go at dawn.

choices.text: Close your eyes, and let it end here

effects.log: You close your eyes in the cart. Nobody in the courtyard knows what you are, except the one who weeps. Afterwards {npc} goes home and lays down the brush and writes no more, and dies two years later, and the last line {he} wrote is that a beast was taken in the western hunt.

events.text: An old scholar pushes through the crowd in the courtyard: {npc}, who has never seen you before. But {his} grandmother tied a ribbon to a beast's horn once, at a birth, and told {him} about it every winter, and {he} sees the ribbon on your horn and knows it. {He} lifts {his} sleeve to {his} face and weeps into it, and says, to nobody: "In an age like this? For whom have you come?"

choices.text: Lift your head, and look at {him}

mem.note: saw the beast with my grandmother's ribbon in the lord's cart

effects.log: {npc} stops weeping. {He} turns to the lord and says, in front of everyone, exactly what the hunt has caught, and what the books say happens to a reign that takes one. The ropes are cut by dusk.

choices.text: Lie still and let the age decide

ok.log: The lord, unnerved by a weeping scholar in the courtyard, has the cart taken back to the hills before dinner, and the rope cut there, and does not watch you go.

fail.log: The lord has the weeping scholar removed and the cart moved into a barn. It is a month before a stable boy, frightened of you and more frightened of what you might mean, leaves the door unbarred. (-10 health)

choices.text: Close your eyes, and let it end here

effects.log: You close your eyes. The scholar weeps until the sleeve is wet through, and goes home, and lays down the brush, and writes no more. The last line {npc} wrote is that a beast was taken in the western hunt, and nobody knew what it was.

events.text: Two kings, an old border, a plain of tall grass between them that nobody has mown in a generation because nobody dares. At dawn the cavalry of both kings will cross it, from the two sides, at a gallop, and meet in the middle, and the grass will be red by noon. You are standing in the middle. You came last night, and nobody saw you come.

choices.text: Stay where you are

effects.log: You stay. At first light the scouts of both sides see something standing in the grass in the middle of the plain, five colours, very still, and ride back to their kings with the same report and the same pale face.

choices.text: Walk the whole plain in the night, so that every blade of it knows you

effects.log: You walk it end to end in the dark without bending a blade. By dawn the whole plain smells of you. The horses of both armies, at the edge of it, will not go in. Their riders do not know why.

events.text: Noon. The horses would not go in at dawn; the kings have had them whipped, and blindfolded, and now the two lines are coming at a walk, then a trot, from both sides, lances down. The ground is shaking. In the middle of the plain there is only you and the grass.

choices.text: Step up onto the air, and let them meet under you, and see each other's faces

effects.log: You rise. The two lines meet in the middle of the plain at a trot, under a beast standing on nothing, and every rider looks up, and stops, and finds himself looking across at the face of a rider on the other side who is also looking up. Nobody lowers a lance. Nobody raises one.

choices.text: Stand, and bear what comes, and live

effects.log: The first horses go round you. The next ones go over you. You do not answer. By the time the line breaks on you, enough riders have seen what they were riding over to stop. You crawl off the plain at dusk with half your ribs broken, and no war that year. (-30 health)

choices.text: Do not move

effects.log: You do not move. They ride over you from both sides, and you do not answer, and when the dust settles the two lines have stopped dead in the middle of the plain, looking at what they have done. The field where you fell is never mown again. No army will cross it. The two kings make peace on its edge, and do not look at each other while they sign.

events.text: The plain of the two kings, a generation on. The grass has grown up taller than a horse. Children from both sides come to the edge of it to dare each other to go in, and do not, and then sit down together in the shade of it and trade rice cakes, because there is nowhere else on the border where both sides can sit.

choices.text: Lie down in the middle, where nobody will see you

effects.log: You lie in the middle of the tall grass all summer and listen to the children at the edges, in two dialects, arguing about whose rice cakes are better. Nobody wins. Everybody eats.

choices.text: Let the children see you once, at dusk

effects.log: Two children from two sides see you stand up in the grass at dusk, and grab each other's hands without thinking. Years later, as old people, they still meet at the edge of the plain every autumn, and neither can remember who grabbed whose hand first.

events.text: A warlord has taken the walls of a city that refused him, and he has said, in front of his captains, that at dawn every soul in it goes to the sword: forty thousand. He does not bluff; you have watched him for years. He sleeps in a tent on the hill with two guards. Nobody can reach him. You can.

choices.text: Go to the tent and speak to him in the bell voice

ok.log: He wakes with a beast of five colours in his tent and listens, because there is nothing else he can do. You speak until the second watch. At dawn the order is changed: the walls come down, not the people. It is not mercy. It is close enough.

fail.log: He listens, and laughs, and calls the guards, who are too frightened to come in. "At dawn," he says, and turns over and goes back to sleep. He is not afraid of anything that will not hurt him. He knows exactly what you are.

choices.text: Go into the city and stand at the gate

effects.log: You walk through the army and into the city by the broken gate and stand there in the dark, facing out. Behind you forty thousand people, who do not know you are there. In front of you, the night, getting shorter. (-10 health)

choices.text: Leave. A qilin cannot save a city

effects.log: You go up onto the cloud and do not look back. You will not forget the lamps in the windows. You were never meant to. In the morning the smoke reaches the clouds, and you do not come down for a long time.

events.text: The last hour before dawn. The warlord is standing in front of his tent in his armour, watching the east for the light. His captains are at the walls. The drums are ready. Only your horn can stop him now: one blow, and the order dies with the man who gave it. You have never struck anything in all your centuries.

choices.text: Stand between him and the city, and bear whatever comes

effects.log: The drums sound. The first rank comes through the broken gate and finds you in it. They do not stop. Neither do you. By the time they are past you there is blood on the gate and you are on your knees, and somewhere in the third rank a soldier throws down a sword and sits in the road, and then another. Half the city lives. (-25 health)

choices.text: Lower your horn and walk away. A vow kept is still a vow

effects.log: You walk away up the hill with your horn unblooded and the drums starting behind you. It is the hardest thing you have ever done, and you are not sure, for the rest of your long life, that it was right. You never will be. That is the cost, and you pay it.

choices.text: Strike once, for the city (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You strike once. The drums never sound. Forty thousand people wake up to an army leaving. And heaven takes your horn, and your colours, one by one, gently, like a mother taking a knife from a child. You live a long life after, as a plain roe deer in the hills above that city, and the city never knows, and you remember, every dawn, that you were something else.

events.text: Years later, a city. It was half burned, once, and has been rebuilt, and the new houses stand among the old ones like young teeth. On the night of the sack every year the people light a lamp in every window and leave the broken gate open, and somebody sweeps the place in front of it where, the old ones say, a beast stood.

choices.text: Stand in the gate again, on the night of the lamps

effects.log: Nobody sees you come. In the morning there are hoofprints in the swept dust, and the city takes it as the best omen in its history, and sweeps the place again, very carefully, around them.

choices.text: Watch from the hill, and count the lamps

effects.log: Twenty-two thousand lamps. You count them all. It is not forty thousand. It is not nothing, either, and you have to stop counting before dawn.

events.text: In the still water below the rapids, the tip of your horn. You have been not looking at it for years. Now you look. The flesh is gone from the last finger's length, and what shows is white and hard, and it does not look like the horn of a beast that harms nothing. It looks like a spearhead.

choices.text: Go and mend what you harmed, one by one

effects.log: A season of finding them, as many as you can name, and some of them old now, who do not know what it is that stands outside their window all one winter. The tip does not soften. But it stops spreading. (Bent -4; -10 health)

choices.text: Look at it a long time, and accept it

effects.log: It is your horn. You did this, one choice at a time, and every one of them had a reason. You do not look away. That is something. It is not enough, and you know that too.

choices.text: Go to the temple above the cave and ask the monks for a cloth to cover it

effects.log: The youngest monk wraps the tip of your horn in clean linen and asks no questions. Under the linen, you can feel it, the bone does not care. But the monks look at you the way they always have, and that matters.

events.text: A warlord's groom on the bank below the cave, with a war saddle and a bridle of red leather. He has been sent, he says, very politely, because his master has heard of a five-coloured beast with a horn like a spearhead, and his master has an army that would follow such a horn into any river. He holds out the bridle. He is very patient.

choices.text: Walk away up the cliff

effects.log: You walk away. The groom does not follow; he does not need to. He leaves the saddle on the bank, in case. Every spring he comes back and oils it.

choices.text: Ask him what his master would use it for

effects.log: "Peace," says the groom, and believes it. "The quickest kind." He describes it: the horn at the head of the column, the enemy breaking without a blow because they see what leads it. It sounds very like what you are for. That is the danger.

choices.text: Let him put the bridle on, to see how it feels

effects.log: It is light. It fits. Something in you that has been tired for a long time lowers its head into it. You shake it off before he can buckle it, but the groom has seen, and he smiles, and goes home to tell his master: soon. (Bent +1)

events.text: The warlord himself on the bank, in armour, with the saddle. Behind him an army that has been beaten twice this year and is looking for something to follow. "You have harmed enough already," he says reasonably, "that a little more will not matter. Carry me, and nobody in my way will dare stand. Fewer will die. You will be what your horn already is."

choices.text: Turn your back on him and walk up into the clouds

effects.log: You turn your back on the army and walk up onto the cloud. The warlord shouts after you for a long time, then sends archers. None of them can bring themselves to shoot at a beast walking away. You do not come down for years.

choices.text: Stand in front of him and say, in the bell voice, what the horn is

ok.log: "Every harm I did," you say, "one at a time." The warlord listens to the whole list. At the end he takes the saddle back himself, and does not send for you again, and fights his war with ordinary horses.

fail.log: He listens, nodding, as if you were confirming a price. "Then one more will not matter," he says, and orders the nets. You are on the cloud before they are spread. The saddle stays on the bank.

choices.text: Lower your head for the saddle

effects.log: You lower your head. The saddle goes on. The warlord rides you into battle, and the armies follow the horn, and the enemy breaks without a blow, just as he said, the first time. After that it is blows. You are only a beast now, a magnificent one, and the grass under you has stopped meaning anything at all.

events.text: A sage you heralded, whose ribbon tore on your horn, has not stopped. Province after province falls to an army that marches under banners painted with you: a scaled beast with a single horn, five colours. "Under the sign of the qilin," they say before each battle. They believe it. Every town that surrenders is told that heaven sent you to bless the conquest.

choices.text: Show yourself in every town before the army reaches it, and walk the other way

effects.log: Town after town sees the beast from the banners walking away from the army, toward the hills. It does not stop the war. It makes the war argue with itself, which is a beginning.

choices.text: Go to the sage at night, as you did when they were small

effects.log: You stand outside the tent of a conqueror you once watched learn to walk. They come out and look at you for a long time. "You promised peace," they say. "I am bringing it." They go back in. (-6 health)

events.text: The conqueror has built a cage of gold before the new throne, tall and beautiful, with a floor of polished jade and a dish of dew changed every dawn by a servant who has been told never to speak to it. The door is open. Heralds read in every square that the qilin is invited to come and take its place, as proof of the virtue of the reign.

choices.text: Stay away. A cage is a cage

effects.log: You stay away. The cage stays empty, and the heralds go on reading the invitation every spring, and the people start to whisper that the qilin has not come because the reign is not worthy. It is the best thing you have ever done by doing nothing.

choices.text: Go to the palace at night and look at the cage

effects.log: It is the most beautiful thing ever made for you. The servant who changes the dew sees you in the dark of the hall and nearly drops the dish, and then, very quietly, against orders, says: "Please do not come in."

events.text: The conqueror has caught you at last: not with nets, with a promise. If you come into the cage, the war stops. The last free provinces will be spared, and their people will live, under a reign that has your image on every banner and you before its throne. If you do not, the war goes on. The conqueror means it. They always did.

choices.text: Refuse, and stand at the border of the last province instead

effects.log: You stand at the border, in front of the army that carries your face on its banners. The soldiers in the front rank look up at their banners, and down at you, and back. The war does not stop. It slows, and it never quite starts again with the same heart. (-20 health)

choices.text: Go back to the cave and grieve, and let the world do what it does

effects.log: You go home. The war goes on without you, as wars do. The cage stays empty before the throne for the whole of the reign, and the people learn to read the empty cage, and it says more than you could.

choices.text: Walk into the cage

effects.log: You walk in. The door closes. The war stops, as promised, and the last provinces are spared, and every envoy who comes to the court is shown the qilin in its cage of gold, proof of the virtue of the reign. You live a very long time. The servant who changes the dew grows old, and is replaced, and the new one does not know you were ever free.

events.text: An age of war. Every province is burning or about to. The omen-readers in every town say the same thing: a beast of five colours seen now means a death, and the hunters are out on every ridge to make sure of it. You have not shown yourself in a long time. Nobody has missed you, that you can tell.

choices.text: Go back to the Qilin Cave and wait for a better age

effects.log: You go home. The straw is old, and smells of nothing now. The rapids are the same. You lie down in the dark and listen to the temple bell, which is still rung every dawn, though the temple is half empty.

choices.text: Go down anyway, unseen, and do what can be done without being seen

effects.log: A season of small things in the dark: a child carried out of a fire, a well cleared, a deserter shown the path home. Nobody sees you. Nobody thanks you. The age does not change. (-8 health)

events.text: The cave. Vines have grown across the mouth since you came back, and in the winter the snow on the ledge outside lies untouched for months. You could stay. Nobody would hunt you. No sage would ever be heralded again, and no ribbon would ever tear.

choices.text: Push through the vines, and go out into the snow

effects.log: The vines tear. The snow takes your hoofprints for the first time in years, and in the morning the monks of the temple find them and stand round them in a ring, saying nothing, for a long time.

choices.text: Stay ten years, and then look again

effects.log: Ten years in the dark, listening to the bell. When you come out, the age is no better. But you are rested, and the hunters have forgotten you, and that will have to do.

choices.text: Stay in the cave, and do not come out again

effects.log: You lie down in the dark of the Qilin Cave and do not come out. The vines grow thicker. The snow lies untouched. Nobody ever hunts you again, and nobody is ever heralded, and the age, eventually, gets better by itself, as ages do, and nobody sees a beast of five colours on the ridge to tell them so. No harm. No song.

events.text: The youngest monk of the temple above the cave, who was a child when you went in, has come down the cliff path every dawn for six years with a bowl of dew, and set it at the vines, and gone back up. Today the monk sits down on the ledge and talks to the vines, as if you were a neighbour who had stopped answering the door.

choices.text: Come out and drink the dew

effects.log: You come out. The monk does not jump, or kneel. The monk says "There you are," and hands you the bowl, and the two of you sit on the ledge above the rapids and watch the sun come up on a bad age.

choices.text: Listen from inside, and do not come out

effects.log: The monk talks for an hour: the temple, the war, the price of rice, a cat. At the end the monk says, "Well. Tomorrow," and goes back up. Tomorrow, you think. Maybe tomorrow.

events.text: A walled town in the south, under a peak to the east of it, the highest hill for a day's walk. Every month the moon comes up over that peak, and the whole town turns to watch it, because it is the best thing they have. Paper makers, fan makers, a market of bean sprouts and rice. No sect, no fortress. A town that has never been worth conquering, and has therefore been conquered nine times.

choices.text: Climb the peak and lie down on it for one night

effects.log: The moon comes up behind you. Down in the town, a paper maker on a roof sees the peak with a lying beast on it, outlined in silver, and calls the whole lane up onto the roofs to look. By morning the peak has a name.

choices.text: Walk through the town at night, through every lane

effects.log: Paper drying on racks in the lanes, white as snow. A smell of bean sprouts. A child awake at a window who sees you and does not tell anyone, for once in the history of children. You think: this is the kind of place that is never safe.

events.text: The town calls it Qilin Peak now, and the moon rising over it the first of the town's famous views. Lovers walk up the lower slope to watch it. An old scholar has written a poem about it that every schoolchild knows. They do not know whether you were real. They do not much mind.

choices.text: Lie on the peak every full moon, for a hundred years

effects.log: A hundred years of full moons. The town grows used to the shape on the peak, and then fond of it, and then sure of it, the way you are sure of a mountain. In those hundred years nobody conquers it, though two armies come close.

choices.text: Lie there only when the town is afraid

effects.log: Plague years, flood years, the year the bandits came: on those nights the moon rises over a lying beast, and the town looks up and is a little less afraid. In good years the peak is only a peak. The town comes to know the difference.

events.text: An army camped on the plain west of the town, its general measuring the walls for the tenth conquest. At moonrise his whole army turns to look east, as the town does, and sees the peak, and on it, against the moon, a beast lying very still, watching them.

choices.text: Stay lying down. Let them look

effects.log: You do not move all night. Neither does the army. In the morning the general strikes camp and marches north, and tells nobody why, and the town never knows how close it was.

choices.text: Stand up on the peak, against the moon

effects.log: You stand. The whole army sees it. Half of them kneel. The general does not kneel, and he does not attack either, and after three days of his soldiers looking at the peak instead of the walls, he goes.

events.text: A quiet age, and the peak above the town has been yours for a lifetime of men. Tonight the full moon comes up behind you as it has so many times, and you feel, for the first time, the peak under you as if it were your own body: the rock, the pines on its shoulder, the spring on its north face. You could lie down, and not get up.

choices.text: Get up, and go on with your life

effects.log: You get up. The town wakes to a peak with no beast on it, and is worried for a month, and then goes back to making paper. You come back sometimes, on full moons, to make sure.

choices.text: Lie down, and become the peak

effects.log: You lie down and do not get up. The peak takes your shape, the way a pillow does, and keeps it. Every night the moon rises over your back, and the town turns to watch it, and has no war for five hundred years, and does not entirely know why, and does not ask.

events.text: A palace embroidery workshop at night. {npc}, the court's best needle, is stitching the badge for a newly named grand prince: a square of dark blue silk, gold thread, a beast with one horn. {He} has stitched forty of them in {his} life and never got the face right. When {he} looks up and sees you in the doorway, {he} does not scream. {He} says, "Hold still."

choices.text: Hold still all night

mem.note: stitched the beast's face from the life

effects.log: You hold still until dawn. {npc} unpicks the face {he} had done and stitches it again, from you. It is the best badge ever worn at that court. {He} never tells anyone how.

choices.text: Ask {him} why a beast for the princes, and not the king

effects.log: "The king has the dragon," says {npc}, threading gold. "The princes are the ones who must wait. Fit to rule, and not allowed to. Who else would you put over their hearts?" {He} bites off the thread. "It is supposed to stop them doing anything stupid."

events.text: A grand prince, young, clever, the king's brother, sitting alone in a dark hall at night with the qilin badge over {his} heart, and a sword across {his} knees. Outside, men are waiting for {his} word to take the palace. {npc} is looking at the sword. Then at the badge. Then up, and you are standing at the end of the hall.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let {him} look at the badge and at you

ok.log: {npc} looks for a long time. Then {he} puts the sword on the floor, and goes out, and sends the men home. In the morning {he} goes to the king's audience as usual, and bows, and waits. {He} waits the rest of {his} life.

fail.log: {npc} looks at you, and then picks up the sword and goes out. The palace is taken by morning. The badge is found later in the hall, unpinned, on the floor, face down.

choices.text: Speak to {him} in the bell voice

effects.log: "The one who waits," you say, and nothing else. {npc} laughs, a short tired laugh, and lays the sword down. "Easy for a beast," {he} says. "You have a thousand years." But {he} waits.

events.text: The old embroiderer's workshop has a new master, who has your face from the old pattern books, and stitches it for every prince of the realm now, not only the grand princes. Badges by the hundred. You could give more than a likeness. You could go into the thread.

choices.text: Leave them only the likeness. Princes must choose for themselves

effects.log: You stay outside the thread. The badges are only badges. Some princes wait and some do not, and it is their own doing either way, which is, you think, the point.

choices.text: Give your image to the badges, and go into them

effects.log: You go into the gold thread. From then on, every prince who wears you over the heart feels it, a small soft pressure like a hoof, when they think of seizing the throne. Most of them wait. Centuries later a badge woven in gold is found in an old tomb, and the scholar who lifts it out feels, for no reason at all, that someone has put a hand on their chest.

events.text: Tomb painters in the north, working in a stone chamber under a hill by lamplight. They paint straight onto the dressed granite, no plaster, so it will last. On the four walls they have finished the guardians, and you know two of them: the blue on the east wall, the white on the west. They have left the ceiling stones for last: lotus, honeysuckle, flying immortals. And one space, among the immortals, the master says is for a beast with one horn.

choices.text: Climb the scaffold and stand for them

effects.log: You stand on a scaffold under the stepped ceiling for a whole winter, very still, among lamps. The master paints you from below, lying on his back on the planks, and talks to you about his children the whole time, as if you were a model he had hired.

choices.text: Ask why above the guardians, and not beside them

effects.log: "The guardians hold the walls," says the master, not looking up from the lotus. "The ones above hold nothing. They only come. That is harder." It is the same thing the Tortoise said, or will say. You stand for him.

events.text: The ceiling is finished. The chamber will be closed tomorrow, with a king in it. The master painter lies on his back on the scaffold one last time and looks at you on the corbel stone, among the immortals, faded already in the lamp smoke. "It needs one more thing," he says, "and I cannot paint it." He means you.

choices.text: Leave them only the painting

effects.log: You climb down. The painting stays, and is very good, and is only paint. The master nods as if he had expected it, and puts out the lamps one by one, and you go out with the last of the painters into the snow.

choices.text: Go into the ceiling stone, and watch the sleeper from above

effects.log: You go into the stone among the lotus and the immortals. They close the chamber. For thirteen hundred years you watch one sleeper from above the dragon and the tiger on the walls, while the colour fades from all of you, and when at last somebody opens the tomb with a lamp, you are the first thing they see when they look up.

events.text: Centuries on, a tomb under a hill in the north is opened by lamplight. The guardians on the walls are faded but still fierce. The people with the lamps look up at the ceiling, at the lotus and the immortals and the beast with one horn, and one of them says it looks as if it is watching. You are standing at the back of the passage.

choices.text: Stay and let them look

effects.log: They look a long time. Nobody turns round. When they leave, the youngest of them bows to the ceiling, very slightly, as if embarrassed to.

choices.text: Go before anyone turns round

effects.log: You go back up the passage into the daylight. Behind you somebody says it is only a painting. Somebody else says, "Yes, but of what?"

events.text: A king of the south is dead, and the royal tomb is being furnished: gold crown, glass cups, a saddle and its flaps, the long mudguards that hang either side of a horse. {npc}, the painter, has a sheet of white birch bark and orders to paint a heavenly horse on it, a horse that gallops in the sky, for the king to ride. {He} has never seen one. Then {he} sees you.

choices.text: Stand for {him}

mem.note: painted the heavenly horse from the life

effects.log: You stand in the workshop for a week. {npc} paints fast, on birch bark, in white and red, with clouds round the border. The legs are galloping. The mane is flying. On the forehead, because {he} paints what {he} sees, a small crescent.

choices.text: Tell {him} you are not a horse

effects.log: "Today you are," says {npc}, already mixing the white. "The king asked for a horse. You are the best horse I have ever seen." You decide not to argue with an artist on a deadline.

events.text: The saddle flaps are done, two of birch bark and one of gilt bronze, and the court has come to look. The court says it is a horse. The court calls it the heavenly horse. One old minister puts a finger on the crescent on its forehead and says, "Horn," and everybody else says, "Mane," and the minister is quiet.

choices.text: Step into the hall, so the old minister can see the horn

effects.log: The court sees you. The court decides, unanimously and immediately, that the painting is of a horse and that this is a different matter. The old minister laughs until the king's son has to help him to a chair.

choices.text: Slip out, and leave them the argument

effects.log: You go. The argument lasts the rest of the reign and comes out, in the end, at mane, by one vote. The old minister writes Horn in the margin of the record, and nobody erases it.

choices.text: Let them call you a horse, and go into the bark

effects.log: You let them call you a horse. The flaps go into the tomb with the king, and the tomb is closed and forgotten, and fifteen hundred years later it is opened and the birch bark is still white. Scholars argue over the crescent on your forehead: horn, or a tuft of mane? They nearly name the tomb after you. In the end they decide it is a horse. You know. You never tell.
