events.text: A herd of ordinary horses in a royal pasture, and among them, by no one's choice, you. The horses think you are a horse. The grooms think you are a horse. A very small child on the fence says, loudly and repeatedly, that the grey one has a horn, and is told to be quiet.

choices.text: Graze among them a season, as a horse

effects.log: Dew off the fence posts, windfall apples, a great deal of standing about. Horses are restful. They argue about nothing but grass. You leave at the end of summer and the herd looks for you for a week.

choices.text: Let the child stroke the horn

effects.log: The child strokes it, and is right, and is told to be quiet again, and goes home triumphant. That child grows up to be very hard to fool, and you suspect you had something to do with it.

events.text: The last shape. You notice it first in a market: a man raises his hand to strike a child who has stolen a persimmon, and the hand stops in the air, and stays there, and he looks at it as if it belonged to somebody else. You are standing at the end of the lane. Where you stand, nobody can raise a hand. It goes as far as you can see.

choices.text: Stay in the market all day, and watch what people do with their hands

effects.log: They do not know what to do with them. A fishmonger who was going to cheat a widow gives her the right change and is furious about it. Two drunks in a doorway, unable to fight, start to sing. By dusk the man with the raised hand has bought the child a persimmon. You did nothing at all.

choices.text: Leave the market quickly. This is too much power for a qilin

effects.log: You leave. Behind you the market goes back to being a market, cheating and shouting and one or two blows. You are not sure it is worse. You are not sure it is better. You will have a thousand years to decide.

events.text: A village where you have lain on the ridge for many years. They have stopped locking doors. The swords that were in the rafters have rusted, and somebody has used three of them as fence posts for the bean field. The children do not know what a raid is. The old people do, and watch the children with a fear that has nowhere to go.

choices.text: Go and lie among the old people, so they can rest

effects.log: The old people of the village sit with you in the evenings on the ridge. They do not say much. One of them, who lost two sons to a raid long ago, falls asleep against your flank, and sleeps a whole night through for the first time since.

choices.text: Leave a little fear in the world. They will need it when you are gone

effects.log: You move further off, to the next ridge. The children learn, from the old people's stories, what a raid was. They still do not lock their doors. But they know why the doors have locks, and you think that is right.

events.text: A war that does not start. Two kingdoms, an old grudge, two young kings who have both made speeches. The armies are on the border. And on the morning of the battle, every soldier on both sides finds that the hand will not close on the hilt. Not fear. They are simply unable to want to.

choices.text: Stay on the border until both armies go home

effects.log: It takes a month. The soldiers sit in the grass. Some of them trade food across the border. The two kings meet in a tent between the lines to find out what is wrong, and come out, after a long time, having made a treaty neither of them remembers proposing.

choices.text: Go away, and let them choose

effects.log: You go. The hands close again on the hilts. And then, slowly, one by one, the soldiers who remember that morning open them. Not all. Enough. The war is short, and small, and the last one for a long time.

events.text: Long ago something told you, or you dreamed it told you, what it is to be the peace and not to bring it. You did not believe it then. You stand on the ridge now in the thousand-year morning and find that you miss the waiting: the gate at dusk, the mother in labour, the ribbon, two nights. Nobody waits for you any more. You are already here.

choices.text: Go and stand at a gate at dusk anyway, where a child is being born

effects.log: A poor house, a lamp, a woman in labour. You stand at the gate as you did for the five. The mother has no ribbon to tie, and does not need one. You stay two nights anyway. The child is not a sage. It is only a child, born into a peace, and that is the whole point.

choices.text: Let the missing be, the way grass lets the wind be

effects.log: You stand in it. It passes through you and does not bend you. In a century it is only a fondness.

events.text: A thousand-year morning. Every land under heaven is quiet at once, which has never happened. No army is marching anywhere. No hand is raised in any market. The meadows from here to the sea are full of dew and not one blade is bent. You could spread yourself over all of it, and stop being a beast.

choices.text: Stay a beast a little longer

effects.log: You fold the morning back up and go and drink at an ordinary stream, among deer who do not run. The thousand-year morning goes by. There will be others. Not many. Enough.

choices.text: Become the peace

effects.log: You lie down across the morning and the morning keeps you. You are no longer a sign of peace. You are the peace. Where you stand, no one can raise a hand, and you stand everywhere, and in a generation nobody remembers why the wars ended, and they do not need to.

events.text: A night with a sliver of moon. You are at the Qilin Cave for the first time in centuries, and the straw smells, impossibly, warm: the way it smelled the night you were born. Down on the Morning-Heaven Stone something bright is going up, a streak of light with a rider on it, and from the back of the cave, where you lay as a foal, comes the sound of something small trying to stand.

choices.text: Go to the back of the cave and look

effects.log: Nothing there but straw, still warm, in the shape of something small. The streak of light is gone. You stand over the hollow in the straw until dawn, remembering the ant on the stone in front of your soft hooves.

choices.text: Watch the light go up from the stone

effects.log: It goes up and up, a beast and a rider, the way you watched it once without knowing what it was. It does not look back. It never did. You understand, at last, that it was not leaving you. It was only going.

events.text: The ghost of the founder's stable-hand is still sweeping the cave floor with a broom of twigs, as it has every night since the night you were born. It stops when it sees you, and leans on the broom. "Big now," it says. "Five colours. They said you would be." It goes back to sweeping. "You know you can start again, if you want. Heaven lets the ones who never harmed anything start again. Not many ask."

choices.text: Ask what you would remember

effects.log: "Everything," says the groom. "That is the trouble with it. You would stand up in the straw a foal again, knowing every ribbon and every grave." It sweeps round your hooves. "Some would call that a gift. I sweep."

choices.text: Ask why it still sweeps

effects.log: "In case," says the groom. "The first one never came back. Neither did he. Somebody has to keep the floor clean for when they do." It does not seem to think this is sad. You find you do not either.

events.text: The same night again, years on: the sliver of moon, the warm straw, the light going up from the stone, the small sound at the back of the cave. It is offering. You could lie down in the hollow in the straw, and wake up small and grey-gold and hornless, with an ant on the stone in front of your hooves, and do it all again, knowing.

choices.text: Stay what you are. Once is the vow

effects.log: You turn away from the hollow and go out onto the ledge. The groom stops sweeping and nods, once, approving or not. Behind you the straw cools, slowly, until it is only straw.

choices.text: Lie down in the hollow, and start again

effects.log: You lie down in the straw, and it is far too small for you, and then it is not. Your legs unfold under you in the dark of the cave and, for the first time, hold. Below, the White Silver Rapids; above, the temple bell. There is an ant on the stone in front of your soft hooves. You remember everything. You step round it.

events.text: A bandit chief has learned what you are. He has tied a merchant's child to a post in the road and sits beside it with a knife. "Strike me," he calls up the hill, delighted. "Go on. One wound and the child goes free. Or keep your pretty vow and watch." He has done this before, to other things that would not fight.
events.arc: The Vow at a Great Height

choices.text: Walk down and stand between the knife and the child

effects.log: You stand there. He cuts you, because he said he would, and keeps cutting, waiting for you to answer. You do not. On the fourth cut his own men pull him away from you, and one of them cuts the rope. (-18 health)

choices.text: Speak to his men in the bell voice, not to him

ok.log: The chief is only one man. His men are twelve, and tired, and some of them have children. You speak to them. By the end of it the chief is sitting alone by the post, and the child is gone, carried off by the youngest of his men, home.

fail.log: The men are too afraid of him. The chief laughs at you all night. At dawn, bored, he lets the child go, and throws a stone at you on his way out. You bear it. (-10 health)

choices.text: Strike him with your horn (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One thrust. He falls back from the post holding his shoulder and screaming, and the child is free, and the bandits scatter. The child stares at you, and at your horn, and runs. (Bent +3)

events.text: A wildfire on the ridge, driven by wind toward a village. The only firebreak in time is the old pine grove on the saddle: you could tear the trees down with your horn and your weight in an hour, and the fire would starve there. The grove is full of nesting birds.
events.arc: The Vow at a Great Height

choices.text: Tear down the grove (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: The trees come down. The fire starves at the gap. The village lives. All night the birds circle over the fallen grove, crying, and you stand among the broken trunks and listen to every one. (Bent +3)

choices.text: Carry the village out instead, family by family, over the cloud

effects.log: You carry them out three at a time on your back, all night, over the smoke. The village burns. Everyone in it lives, and so does every bird in the grove. They will have to build again. They are alive to build. (-15 health)

choices.text: Stand in the fire's path at the edge of the village and call the rain

ok.log: There is no rain to call. But there is a cloud, and you are standing on its shadow, and you ask it, and somewhere in the east a storm that likes you hears. The fire goes out at the first houses.

fail.log: Nothing answers. You stand in the smoke until the villagers drag you out with them as they run. Half the village burns. Nobody dies. (-12 health)

events.text: A starving tigress has followed you for three days, with two cubs. She cannot catch anything; she is too weak. Every evening she lies down at a distance and looks at you, and then at the roe deer that graze unafraid in your shadow, because the beasts do not bolt near you. She is asking. If you step away, the deer will run, and she can hunt.
events.arc: The Vow at a Great Height

choices.text: Step away from the deer (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You walk off up the ridge. Behind you the deer remember they are deer, and run, and one of them does not run fast enough. The cubs eat. You did not touch anything. You know exactly what you did. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Stay. Lead her to the carcass of a winter-killed elk instead

effects.log: It takes you two days to find it, frozen under a drift on the north slope. You dig it out with your hooves. The tigress eats, and the cubs, and nothing died for it that had not died already. (-6 health)

choices.text: Stay, and do nothing

effects.log: You stay among the deer. On the fourth evening the tigress gets up and goes away, very slowly, with the cubs. One cub, in the spring, is alone. You think about that cub for a long time.

events.text: A man kneels in the road in front of you and asks you to kill the man who broke him. He shows you the scars. That man is a magistrate's man in the next town, free, smiling, and has done it to nine others. "You are heaven's beast," the man says. "Is heaven only for not doing things?"
events.arc: The Vow at a Great Height

choices.text: Go to that man's door and stand outside it for a year

effects.log: Every morning the man opens the door and you are there. Every evening. The neighbours begin to gather to look. At the end of the year he leaves the town, and the job, and the province, and nobody sees him again. It is not justice. It is something. (-8 health)

choices.text: Answer him honestly: yes, mostly, and it is not enough

effects.log: He stares at you. Then he gets up off his knees. "Then I will do it," he says, and you cannot stop him without harming him, and you do not. You do not find out how it ends. That is part of the cost.

choices.text: Do as he asks (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You go to the next town at night. In the morning the magistrate's man is dead, and the town does not grieve, and the man from the road weeps with relief. In the still water of the well, the tip of your horn is whiter than it was yesterday. (Bent +10)

events.text: Summer on the cloud. A mosquito has found you, the only one ever to fly this high, and it has been drinking from the soft place behind your ear every evening for a month. It is very small. It is very persistent. It sings.
events.arc: The Vow at a Great Height

choices.text: Let it drink

effects.log: It drinks all summer and grows fat and sluggish and very pleased with itself. In the autumn it dies of old age in the fur behind your ear, the most travelled mosquito in history. You miss the singing, a little.

choices.text: Flick your ear, carefully, so it moves on without being hurt

ok.log: It moves to your flank. Then your other ear. You have a long talk with yourself about patience, and lose.

fail.log: Your ear flicks harder than you meant. The singing stops. You look at the small thing on the cloud for a long time. It counts. Everything counts. (Bent +1)

events.text: Two sect masters fighting on a cliff path, both very good, both bleeding. One slips and catches the edge with one hand. The other raises a sword over the hand. You are close enough to knock the sword away, which would send its owner off the cliff instead.
events.arc: The Vow at a Great Height

choices.text: Knock the sword away (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One sweep of your head. The sword goes over the edge, and so does the one holding it. You pull the other one up by the collar with your teeth. They stare at you, and at the place where their enemy was, and say nothing at all. (Bent +10)

choices.text: Put your own neck between the sword and the hand

effects.log: The sword comes down on your neck. It does not go through; you are very old and very scaled. The swordsman stares at the beast that took the blow. The one on the edge climbs up. Neither of them fights again that day, or that year. (-20 health)

choices.text: Say one word in the bell voice

ok.log: "No." The sword stops. Its owner looks at you, and down at the hand on the edge, and after a long moment reaches down and pulls the other up. They sit on the path, panting, and start to laugh.

fail.log: The sword falls, and you take it on your neck after all, lunging into the gap. You bleed. They both live. (-15 health)

events.text: Something small underfoot, again. The path is narrow, wet, crowded with snails after rain, and you are very large now and very old and very tired, and you have been stepping round snails for centuries.
events.arc: The Vow at a Great Height

choices.text: Step round every one, as always

ok.log: Every one. It takes the whole night to go a mile. At dawn a farmer finds the path covered in snails and one long line of hoofprints threading between them, and does not understand what he is looking at, and tells his grandchildren anyway.

fail.log: One. In the dark, on the wet stone, one small crunch. You stand still for a long time. Centuries, and it is still one at a time. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Step up onto the air and go over them

effects.log: You go over them on the air. It is easier. You are not sure it is better. The snails, as far as you can tell, have no opinion.

events.text: A demonic sect has heard that a qilin that kills is a weapon, and a qilin that has killed once will kill again. They have taken a whole village and stood it in the square, and their master says, very reasonably, that they will let one go for every blade of grass you bend. "Bend a hundred," the master says. "It is only grass."
events.arc: The Vow at a Great Height

choices.text: Bend the grass for them, blade by blade (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You trample the meadow before the square, a blade for a villager, while the sect watches and laughs. One by one the villagers go. It is only grass. It is the first grass you have broken on purpose in all your centuries, and it is very much more than grass. (Bent +3)

choices.text: Lie down in front of the square, and wait them out

effects.log: You lie down. You wait. They threaten, and then do some of the things they threatened, and you bear the ones done to you, and the village, watching you bear it, stops being afraid of them. On the ninth day the sect leaves. They cannot rule a square that is not afraid. (-15 health)

choices.text: Speak to the sect master alone, in the bell voice

ok.log: You speak to the master for a night. In the morning the master lets the village go, all of it, and walks away from the sect alone, and is found years later teaching children to read in a hill town, very badly, and very gently.

fail.log: The master listens with great interest and takes notes. Then the master lets half the village go, as a courtesy, and keeps the rest. You stay until the rest are free. It takes a year. (-10 health)

events.text: A poor house at dusk, a lamp in the window, and the sound you have learned to know across the centuries: a woman in labour, and an old woman telling her to breathe. You do not know yet if the child is a sage. You never know until the ribbon.
events.arc: A Mother in Labour at Dusk

choices.text: Stand at the gate, and see

effects.log: You stand at the gate until the child cries. Nobody comes out with a ribbon. It is a child, only a child, red and furious. You stay the two nights anyway. Some of the best people you ever knew were only children. (Herald a Birth, when your heart says it is the one.)

choices.text: Stay in the dark, and only listen

effects.log: You listen from the trees. A long labour, a healthy cry, a mother laughing at nothing. You leave before dawn. There will be other gates.

events.text: An omen-reader in a hard age has worked out the pattern: a beast at a gate means a sage. So now, in this province, every rich house with a woman near her time has its gate thrown open and a ribbon ready, and servants with nets in the bushes, in case.
events.arc: A Mother in Labour at Dusk

choices.text: Go to a poor house instead, three valleys away

effects.log: Three valleys away there is a poor house with no nets and no servants, and a mother who does not know what you are and ties a scrap of her own skirt to your horn because the old women say you must. The rich houses wait all winter.

choices.text: Walk past every rich gate in the province, slowly, and stop at none

effects.log: You walk past them all. The nets come out and close on nothing. The omen-reader's pattern is ruined, and the omen-reader with it, and the rich houses of the province never quite trust a ribbon again.

events.text: Alchemists of the high realms have woven a net of heaven-silk, finer than mist, and spread it across the sky between three peaks, because a qilin that walks on cloud must cross the sky somewhere. The tip of a qilin's horn, their old books say, ground with dew, gives a hundred years.
events.arc: The Horn-Takers of the High Realms

choices.text: Go down and walk the long way, on the ground, as you used to

effects.log: You come down and walk on the earth again for a season, carefully, as you did when you were young. The net waits in the sky for a year, catching cranes, which the alchemists let go in a fury.

choices.text: Walk into the net and lie still in it until they come

effects.log: They come up the peaks at dawn with knives and bowls. They find you lying in the net looking at them. They stand there a long time. Then the eldest of them sits down on the rock and puts the knife away and asks you, quite humbly, how long a hundred years actually feels. (-6 health)

choices.text: Tear the net with your horn (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One sweep and the heaven-silk parts like smoke. One of the alchemists, holding the far end on a peak, goes down the scree with it. Not far. Far enough. (Bent +1)

events.text: {npc}, an alchemist of great age and greater courtesy, has come up the mountain alone with a silver knife and a silk cloth. "Only the tip," {he} says. "A sliver. You would not miss it. My master is dying, and has been kind to me for two hundred years."
events.arc: The Horn-Takers of the High Realms

choices.text: Lower your head and let {him} take a sliver (this will bend the grass)

mem.note: gave me the tip of your horn

effects.log: It hurts more than you expected. The tip of your horn is flesh, and {npc} weeps as {he} cuts it. {He} goes down the mountain with a sliver in the silk. You do not know whether it worked. The flesh grows back, slowly, a little paler. (Bent +1; -10 health)

choices.text: Go down the mountain with {him}, to the master

effects.log: You go down with {npc} to the master's bedside. The master looks at you, and laughs, and says the horn would not have worked, the books are wrong, but this is better. The master dies that night, smiling. {npc} keeps the silver knife and never uses it again.

choices.text: Refuse, gently

effects.log: {npc} bows. "I thought you would," {he} says. "I had to ask." {He} goes down the mountain. You stand on the cloud a long time afterwards, not sure you were right.

events.text: Hunters again, at the cave mouth, in an age when hunters are paid well: they have set poisoned salt-licks along the path to the rapids, and the deer of the valley are finding them first.
events.arc: The Horn-Takers of the High Realms

choices.text: Lie across the path all night so the deer cannot reach the salt

effects.log: The deer come in the dark and find you lying across the path, and stand there, puzzled, and go back to the forest. In the morning you push every lick into the rapids with your nose. (-8 health)

choices.text: Lead the hunters to the licks, in the bell voice, and make them clear them

ok.log: They clear every lick, sweating, while a beast of five colours watches them. Then they go home and find other work. One of them becomes the best beekeeper in the province.

fail.log: They run before you finish the first sentence and leave the licks. You push them into the rapids yourself, all night.

events.text: A soul at the river of the dead, at the ford where the souls cross, and it cannot cross: an old fisherman who spent his life on water and is afraid of this one. He has been standing on the bank for nine years. The other souls go round him.

choices.text: Kneel, and carry him over on your back

effects.log: He climbs on, very cautious, the way fishermen get into other people's boats. Halfway over he starts to tell you about the best catch of his life. By the far bank he has forgotten to be afraid. He gets off without looking back, which is how it should be.

choices.text: Walk across first, slowly, so he can see it holds

effects.log: You walk over and back, over and back, on the dark water. On the ninth crossing he steps onto the river behind you, and it holds him too, and he walks across on his own two feet, laughing like a boy.

events.text: Refugees on the bank of a river in flood, and soldiers coming behind them on the road. No boats. Three hundred people, mostly old and very young, and the water brown and fast and wide.

choices.text: Walk ahead of the column on the water, and let them follow

ok.log: You step out onto the flood and it holds you, and when the first child follows you, it holds the child. All three hundred cross on the water behind you, dry to the ankle. The soldiers reach the bank and stand there with their mouths open.

fail.log: It holds most of them. A boy slips at the middle and you go into the brown water after him and come out with him in your teeth by his collar, and the river takes a great deal out of you. Everyone crosses. (-12 health)

choices.text: Carry them over on your back, a few at a time

effects.log: All night, back and forth, three and four at a time. At dawn the last of them is over and the soldiers are on the far bank, too late, and you are lying on the shingle unable to stand. A grandmother covers you with her shawl. (-15 health)

events.text: A dying old king asks, as they do now that the story has got around, to be carried up, as the first king was. He is not a founder. He inherited everything and was neither cruel nor kind. He is very frightened.

choices.text: Carry him to his grandchildren instead

effects.log: "Not yet," you tell him. You carry him on your back across the palace to the room where his grandchildren are sleeping, and set him down among them. He dies there in the morning, holding a small hand, not frightened at all.

choices.text: Carry him as far as the clouds, and let him see his kingdom once

effects.log: He sees it all from the clouds: the roads, the river, the villages. "So small," he says. "I should have been kinder. It was so small." You bring him down. He lives a year more, and is kinder, and it is noticed.

events.text: A lost soul at a crossroads in the mountains: a child, drowned in a spring flood a century ago, still standing where the road forks, waiting for a mother who went the other way. The villagers have built a little shrine there. Nobody knows the child is still in it.

choices.text: Carry the child across, to where the mother went

effects.log: You kneel at the crossroads and the child climbs on, light as a leaf. You take the other fork, the one the mother took, a long way, further than roads go. At the end of it someone is waiting, and has been, for a century. You do not stay to watch. You do not need to.

choices.text: Stay with the child at the shrine for a year first

effects.log: A year at a crossroads with a ghost child, who tells you everything about the spring flood and the mother and a dog called Chestnut. At the end of the year the child says, all by itself, "I can go now," and you carry it.

events.text: A human who stands at your level, which almost no human does: {npc}, a grandmaster of the divine realms, who has walked to the cave on foot and sits down on the Morning-Heaven Stone like a pilgrim. "I have killed nine hundred people," {he} says. "Every one of them in a fair fight. It is how I came this high. How did a beast that never fought get this far?"

choices.text: "By not getting out of the way"

mem.note: asked the beast how it climbed so high without a fight

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it for a whole day on the stone. "That is harder," {he} says at last. "Much harder. I would not have managed it." {He} leaves at dusk, and you hear later that {he} never draws a sword again.

choices.text: Ask {him} about the nine hundred, one at a time

effects.log: {npc} starts, and stops at the fortieth, and cannot go on. {He} did not know {he} remembered them. You sit with {him} on the stone until dawn. {He} goes away very quietly, a long way short of nine hundred.

choices.text: "Slowly. A blade at a time"

effects.log: {npc} laughs out loud. "A blade at a time," {he} says. "I did it a head at a time." {He} looks at {his} hands. "Yours lasts longer."

events.text: {npc}, an old general, lame now, finds you on the ridge above a plain where two armies once faced each other. "I was the one who lowered my banner first," {he} says. "I have been dishonoured for it for forty years. My own sons will not speak of it. Was I a coward?"

choices.text: "You were the bravest man on the field"

mem.note: said I was the bravest on the field

effects.log: {npc} weeps on the ridge, in the open, like a boy. Then {he} goes home and tells {his} sons, in the bell voice's exact words, and they listen, because who would invent that.

choices.text: "You were afraid, and you lowered it anyway. That is the whole of courage"

effects.log: {npc} is quiet a long time. "Afraid of you," {he} says. "No," you say. "Afraid of what you would be if you did not." {He} nods slowly. {He} has known it for forty years. {He} needed to hear it said aloud.

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court, {npc}, in plain clothes, on the cloud beside you at dusk, travelling ahead of a decision. "Off the record," {he} says. "The court is asking whether the qilin should come down to the world at all, in an age like this one. A beast that can only appear in peace, in an age of war. Should you?"

choices.text: "Only where it is safe for others. Never where it is only safe for me"

effects.log: {npc} writes it down, and then crosses it out, and writes it again in a better hand. "The court will not like that," {he} says. "It has no rule in it." "No," you say.

choices.text: "Yes. Especially in an age like this one"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "They will hunt you," {he} says. "They always have," you say. {npc} puts away the brush. "Off the record," {he} says, "good."

choices.text: "Ask the people of this age, not the court"

effects.log: {npc} goes down into the world in plain clothes for a year and asks. Most people have never heard of a qilin. The ones who have all say the same thing: come. {npc} takes that back to the Jade court, and it causes trouble there for a century.

events.text: {npc}, an immortal sovereign of a court in the high heavens, has come down with a retinue to make you an offer: a cage of gold, a floor of jade, dew from the heavenly peaches every morning, a place before {his} throne. "As proof," {he} says pleasantly, "of the virtue of my reign. You would want for nothing."

choices.text: Decline, and walk away over the clouds

effects.log: {npc} does not take no. For a century {his} messengers find you on every cloud with a better cage. For a century you walk away. In the end {he} has a qilin carved in jade before the throne and tells visitors it is the real one, turned to stone by {his} virtue.

choices.text: Ask {him} whether a reign that needs proof is virtuous

effects.log: {npc} opens {his} mouth, and shuts it. {His} retinue look at their feet. "No," {he} admits at last. {He} goes home, and has the cage melted down, and spends the gold on something nobody writes about, which is the best thing a sovereign can do with gold.

events.text: {npc}, an heir. Not a sage of yours: an ordinary prince's heir, clever, impatient, wearing the qilin badge over {his} heart because it came with the rank. {He} has climbed the ridge to find you, to ask the one thing nobody at court will answer: "How long must I wait? My father is cruel. I could end it in a night."

choices.text: "Longer than you can bear. Bear it"

effects.log: {npc} goes white. Then {he} laughs, unhappily. "That is what the badge says," {he} says, touching it, "if you listen to it." {He} goes back down. {He} waits. It is eleven years. {He} is a good king, when it comes.

choices.text: "End the cruelty, not the king"

ok.log: {npc} thinks about it the whole way down the mountain. Within a year {he} has quietly freed half the prisons in {his} father's name, and the father, who never reads anything, signs it all. It is not a revolution. It is better.

fail.log: {npc} hears what {he} wants to. A year later there is a palace coup, very bloody, and {he} wears the badge to the coronation. You will not go near that court for a reign.

events.text: {npc}, a heavenly immortal, comes to the cloud with a question from the Four Spirits' court, which has asked {him} for testimony. "I lived below for eighty years," {he} says, "in the valleys where you walked. They have asked me: did the qilin ever bend the grass? I must answer truthfully. I am asking you first, as a courtesy."

choices.text: "Tell them everything you saw"

effects.log: {npc} nods. {He} tells them everything: the meadows, the sages, and the grass that stood wherever you had been. The serpent writes it in red, and then in black, and cannot decide.

choices.text: "Tell them you never saw me"

effects.log: "That is true," says {npc}. "In a few years, I never once saw you. I only saw the grass standing." {He} tells the court exactly that, and the Yellow Dragon, which was asleep, says "Good," without opening its eyes.

events.text: Two sect leaders at a ford, the same ford, the same quarrel, the third generation of it. Their grandfathers quarrelled here and you stopped them with one sentence. Their fathers quarrelled here and you stopped them with two. {npc}, the elder of the two, sees you coming over the water and sighs. "Again?"

choices.text: "Again"

effects.log: One sentence. They put up their swords. {npc} laughs before {he} can stop it. "My grandfather told me about you," {he} says. "The old one said you would be bored of us by now." You are not. You never are. That is the trick.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let them hear their grandfathers instead

ok.log: You stand in the ford in silence. After a while {npc} says, "My grandfather said", and stops, and the other says, "So did mine," and they find that their grandfathers said the same thing. The quarrel ends for good.

fail.log: They fight round you in the ford for an hour, very carefully not touching the beast in the middle. In the end they are too tired to go on and go home. Next time, then. (-8 health)

events.text: A bandit chief on a mountain road, {npc}, who has heard that you talk and has come to argue. "You tell people not to fight," {he} says, "because you cannot. Easy for a beast with no enemies. I was born in a ditch. The sword is the only thing that ever fed me."

choices.text: Tell {him} you were born in a cave, and fed on what fell

effects.log: {npc} listens to the whole story, the windfall chestnuts and the dew and the winter with nothing fallen. "You starved," {he} says. "Often," you say. {He} looks at {his} sword a long while. {He} sells {his} horse that spring and buys a field.

choices.text: Agree with {him}, and ask what {he} would need instead

effects.log: {npc} was ready for a sermon, not a question. {He} answers it: land, a roof, people who will not spit at {him}. It takes you ten years to find all three. You find them.

events.text: {npc}, a sovereign of the Upper Realm with a world in {his} keeping that has never had a single quiet year, has come to ask the Great Peace for itself. "Come and stand in my world," {he} says. "One year. Let them see what it is. They do not believe it exists."

choices.text: Go, and stand in that world for a year

mem.note: brought the Great Peace to my world for a year

effects.log: One year, in a world that has never had a quiet one. At first nobody knows what to do with their hands. By the end of it a generation of children has grown up thinking peace is a normal thing to have. They will fight for it now, which is a strange thing to leave behind. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell {him} peace cannot be borrowed. It has to grow

effects.log: {npc} is disappointed, and then, slowly, interested. You talk for a century about what grows it: the sages, the ribbons, a blade at a time. {He} goes home with a list, and the list is very short, and very hard.

events.text: An army on the only road to a valley you know well. It has stopped because you are standing in the road. The general rides to the front and looks at you for a long time. "Move," he says, "or be moved."

choices.text: Do not move

effects.log: You do not move. They try to move you: ropes, then horses, then spear butts. You bear all of it. By evening the general is sitting on a rock looking at you, and by morning the army has gone round by the long road, and the valley has two more weeks to get its people into the hills. (-15 health)

choices.text: Step aside, and walk ahead of them into the valley, so the villages are warned

effects.log: You step aside and go ahead of them up the road at a run. The villages see you coming and know what is coming behind you. By the time the army arrives, the valley is empty, the granaries hidden, and there is nothing to burn but empty houses.

events.text: Two sects are at war over a mountain pass and its toll, and the pass runs past your old cave. This morning their vanguards met at the Morning-Heaven Stone, and stopped, because it seemed wrong to fight on it, and are standing there now on either side of the old hoofprints, glaring.

choices.text: Come out of the cave and stand on the stone between them

effects.log: You come out and stand in your own hoofprints. Nobody on either side draws. After an hour the two vanguard captains, both very young, sit down on the stone on either side of you, and you understand that they were waiting for an excuse.

choices.text: Ring the temple bell above, in the bell voice

ok.log: The bell and your voice together. Every sword on the stone goes back into its sheath without anyone deciding it should. The war is not over. But it is not going to be fought on that stone.

fail.log: The bell rings. They look up. Then they go on glaring, but further down the path, off the stone. It is a start.

events.text: The omen-readers of a hard age are out in every market: a beast of five colours seen now means a death, and they have a list of whose. People are buying charms against you, little paper beasts with their horns crossed out.

choices.text: Stay out of sight until the age turns

effects.log: You stay on the clouds. The charms sell for a year and then stop selling, because nobody has seen you, and the omen-readers go back to reading the weather, which is safer.

choices.text: Show yourself in the market, and let nobody die

effects.log: You walk through the biggest market in the province at noon. Everyone sees you. Nobody dies that week, or that month, or that year, on the list or off it. The omen-readers have a very bad year. The charm sellers have a worse one.

events.text: Since you took the seat, the furred beasts of the world do not bolt from you. They do not bolt much from anything, in a good age. This year a hunter in the north came home empty-handed every day of the season because the deer would walk up to him and look at him, and he could not do it.

choices.text: Go and find the hunter, and see that the family eats

effects.log: You lead him, over a season, to the things that fall: windfall chestnuts, a valley of wild mushrooms after rain, a stream where the fish are too many. His family eats. He never hunts again, and is not sorry.

choices.text: Let it be. A good age has its costs too

effects.log: The hunter becomes a charcoal burner. His son becomes a hunter, in a worse age, when the deer run again. Ages turn. You were never meant to stop them, only to be a sign of the good ones.

events.text: The chief of the furred beasts, the old books call you: of the three hundred and sixty, the first. Every creature with fur has come, in the end, to this meadow below the cave to look at you once. Today it is a very old bear, so old it has gone grey, who sits down at the edge of the meadow and does not leave.

choices.text: Sit with the bear until it is ready

effects.log: Three days. The bear does not want anything. It only wanted to see. On the third evening it lies down at the edge of the meadow and does not get up, and you stand over it all night, as you stood over the sages, though it had no ribbon.

choices.text: Walk the bear home, to its own mountain

effects.log: It takes a month at the bear's pace. You walk beside it to its own mountain and its own cave, and it goes in, and you hear it settle. In the spring it does not come out. That is the right way round.

events.text: A tiger, two ridges over, who used to be very embarrassed about lying down facing south when the Spirits called you, has come to complain. It cannot hunt in your valley. Nothing runs. "It is unsporting," it says, "and I am hungry, and you have ruined three good ridges."

choices.text: Show it the next valley, where things still run

effects.log: You walk it to the edge of your peace and show it the valley beyond, where the deer still bolt like deer. It goes down, muttering. In the spring it comes back to the ridge to sleep in the sun, where nothing will disturb it, which it says is the only thing you are good for.

choices.text: Apologise, and mean it

effects.log: The tiger is so surprised that it forgets to be angry. It lies down next to you on the ridge, and after a while says that nobody has ever apologised to a tiger before, and that it is not sure it likes it, and falls asleep.

events.text: A ghost at the cave mouth at dawn, thin as the steam off a rice pot: one of your sages, who died while you were far away, or asleep, or hunted, with the ribbon still on your horn. "I waited," the ghost says, not unkindly. "Right to the end. I thought you would come. I wanted you to know I was not angry. Only surprised."

choices.text: Tell the ghost where you were, and why

effects.log: It listens. "A good reason," it says. "There is always a good reason. That is what I was surprised by." It is gone before you can answer, and the faded ribbon on your horn lifts once in a wind that is not blowing.

choices.text: Lower your head and say nothing

effects.log: You lower your head until the faded ribbon touches the ground in front of the ghost. It looks at the ribbon a long time. Then it touches it, once, with fingers you cannot feel, and is not there.

choices.text: Ask it to come with you to the next birth of its colour

effects.log: It comes. When you stand at the next gate where a child of its colour is being born, a thin shape stands beside you in the dusk, watching. When the child cries, the ghost smiles, and goes, at last.

events.text: The village where a sage of yours died alone has built a shrine to them: a plain wooden hall with their brush and their sandals on the altar. On the lintel the villagers have carved: the beast did not come. Every child in the village bows to it. They have made a virtue out of your absence.

choices.text: Come at the spring rite, and stand at the shrine door

effects.log: The rite stops. A whole village in their best clothes looks at a five-coloured beast in the door of a shrine that says it never came. Nobody knows what to do. A child starts to laugh, and then everybody is laughing, and then weeping, and the lintel stays exactly as it is.

choices.text: Leave it. They need the absence more than the beast

effects.log: You leave it. A lintel that says you never came has made the children of that village kinder to the dying than you could have by coming. You go and see each of them at the end, for a century, as a kind of apology nobody asked for.

events.text: A year of the long peace. Children are flying kites over the rice paddies, a hundred of them, and one has got loose and is going up and up toward the ridge where you lie, its string trailing.

choices.text: Catch the string in your teeth and bring it back down

effects.log: You walk down into the paddies with the kite string in your teeth and give it back to a very small child, who says thank you and does not seem to find any of this unusual. In the long peace, children do not.

choices.text: Let it go up, and see where it lands

effects.log: It goes over three ridges and lands in another valley, where a different child finds it and keeps it. Nobody fights about it. It is that kind of year.

events.text: A year of the long peace. A sword sect has run out of enemies, and its disciples practise their forms in the courtyard every morning against nothing, very beautifully, and the sect master has started teaching them to dance instead, because the forms were always half dance anyway.

choices.text: Watch the forms from the wall

effects.log: It is very beautiful. Nobody is hurt. Long ago these forms were for killing, and the bodies still remember, and in the long peace they have turned the memory into something else. You watch every morning for a year.

choices.text: Go down into the courtyard and dance with them

effects.log: Twelve disciples and a beast of five colours in a courtyard at dawn. You are terrible at it. They are very polite about it. The master writes a new form that year, called the Qilin Who Cannot Dance, and it becomes the sect's favourite.

events.text: A year of the long peace, and somewhere in it, very small, a quarrel: two farmers over a boundary stone, shouting in a field. In the long peace they cannot raise a hand. They are shouting all the louder for it.

choices.text: Let them shout. Shouting is allowed

effects.log: They shout all afternoon. At dusk they are both hoarse, and one of them starts laughing, and the other cannot help it, and they move the stone back half a step each. Peace was never meant to be quiet.

choices.text: Stand by the stone until they notice you

effects.log: They notice you in the middle of a sentence and stop. The rest of the quarrel is conducted in whispers, very politely, with frequent bows in your direction, and is settled by supper.

events.text: A year of the long peace, and the old people of the valleys have started to forget what war was. They tell the children about it the way they tell about goblins, half laughing. One very old woman still remembers properly, and comes up to the ridge to sit with you, because you are the only other one who does.

choices.text: Remember it with her, out loud

effects.log: You tell each other all of it, all afternoon, the burnings and the armies and the hard ages. It is terrible to say aloud. At the end she says she feels lighter, and goes down the hill, and tells her great-grandchildren one true story, and only one, which is enough.

choices.text: Let her forget, gently

effects.log: You lie beside her on the ridge and say nothing about war. She talks about her garden instead. By the end of the summer she is laughing about goblins with the children. Some things should be allowed to end.

events.text: A year of the long peace, and a hard one in it, which happens: a drought in the south, and hunger, and in the hunger the first raised hand in a long age, a man stealing grain who strikes the watchman. The whole province hears about it as if it were a comet.

choices.text: Go south and walk among the hungry

effects.log: You walk the dry fields for a season. Granaries open. Wells are shared. The man who struck the watchman goes to the watchman's house with a sack of his own grain the next year, and the watchman takes it, and they never speak of it again. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let the age find its own way through

effects.log: The province finds its way, slowly, badly in places. You watch. It is not your peace if it cannot survive one dry year without you. It survives. Not easily. It survives.
